title: How do we compare five pairs of fractions and justify each answer?
description: Five pairs of fractions are compared by writing both fractions of a pair with the same fractional unit and then comparing the top numbers. The board finishes with a check using a different common unit for the first pair.
teaching_notes: One idea: write both fractions with the same bottom number, then the one with more of that unit is greater. Watch for students who compare the top numbers before the bottom numbers match.

video_script.why: A learner compares fractions by the method of the solved example: find a common multiple of the bottom numbers, rewrite both fractions, and compare the top numbers.
video_script.substitution: the book's own five pairs of fractions
video_script.anchor: five pairs of fractions written on the board
video_script.payoff_line: each answer is justified by the same fractional unit

final_answer.spoken: each answer is justified by the same fractional unit, and only the last pair has the first fraction less

video_script.fraction_reading: eight thirds, five halves, four ninths, three sevenths, seven tenths, nine fourteenths, twelve fifths, eight fifths, nine fourths
never_show: a comparison made on top numbers alone when the bottom numbers differ
maths_rules: 12/5 and 8/5: the bottom numbers match; 12 > 8, so 12/5 > 8/5
video_script.design: Five pairs stay on the board. Each pair is rewritten with one bottom number, as in the solved examples, and the top numbers are compared. The check uses twelve for the first pair.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, and it has five pairs of fractions.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>In each pair, we must say which fraction is greater and give a reason.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can we justify each answer?

beats.on_screen: the five pairs hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: two fractions with the same bottom number are lined up as pieces of the same size, and the one with more pieces is longer

marks.more: the one with more pieces is longer and is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>When two fractions use the same fractional unit, their pieces are the same size.
<bookmark mark='more'/>Then the fraction with more pieces is the greater one.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are five pairs of fractions.

beats.on_screen: To find: the greater fraction in each pair, with a reason
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the greater fraction in each pair, and justify the answer.

marks.six: 8/3 and 5/2 are written and 6 is circled
marks.cmp: 8/3 changes to 16/6, 5/2 changes to 15/6, and 16 and 15 are compared

beats.colours: the common bottom number = accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>Step one, we use the same way as the solved example in your book. Find a common multiple, rewrite both fractions, and compare the top numbers.
<bookmark mark='six'/>For eight thirds and five halves, six is a common multiple.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>Eight thirds is sixteen sixths, and five halves is fifteen sixths. Sixteen is more than fifteen, so eight thirds is greater.

marks.sixtythree: 4/9 and 3/7 are written and 63 is circled
marks.cmp: 4/9 changes to 28/63, 3/7 changes to 27/63, and 28 and 27 are compared

beats.colours: the common bottom number = accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='sixtythree'/>Step two, take four ninths and three sevenths. Nine times seven is sixty-three.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>Four ninths is twenty-eight sixty-thirds, and three sevenths is twenty-seven sixty-thirds. Twenty-eight is more, so four ninths is greater.

marks.count: 7/10 and 9/14 are written and the multiples 14, 28, 42, 56, 70 are listed
marks.cmp: 7/10 changes to 49/70, 9/14 changes to 45/70, and 49 and 45 are compared

beats.colours: the common bottom number = accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step three, take seven tenths and nine fourteenths. Count in fourteen until ten fits, and seventy works.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>Seven tenths is forty-nine seventieths, and nine fourteenths is forty-five seventieths. Forty-nine is more, so seven tenths is greater.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 12/5 and 8/5: the bottom numbers are already equal; compare 12 and 8; 12 > 8

marks.same: 12/5 and 8/5 are written with the same bottom number circled

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step four, twelve fifths and eight fifths already have the same bottom number.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>We compare twelve and eight. Twelve is more, so twelve fifths is greater.

marks.four: 9/4 and 5/2 are written and 4 is circled
marks.cmp: 5/2 changes to 10/4, and 9 and 10 are compared

beats.colours: the common bottom number = accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='four'/>Step five, take nine fourths and five halves. Two goes into four, so use four.
<bookmark mark='cmp'/>Five halves is ten fourths. Nine is less than ten, so nine fourths is less than five halves.

beats.on_screen: Check: use 12 for the first pair: 8/3 = 32/12 and 5/2 = 30/12; 32 > 30, the same answer

marks.same: 32 and 30 are compared and the same pair of answers is ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='twelve'/>Step six, check the first pair with twelve. Eight thirds is thirty-two twelfths, and five halves is thirty twelfths.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Thirty-two is more than thirty, so we get the same answer with a different common unit.

marks.ans: the five results are written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each answer is justified by the same fractional unit. Only in the last pair is the first fraction less.
